subtopic: Friend succeeds when you are struggling
passage:
In the library at Manchester, Chen kept a small table in his notebook: Oskar's class rank, Oskar's internship offers, Oskar's package from the consulting firm, and a column for himself. The gap always ran the wrong way.

On Thursday Oskar left a folder of lecture notes on the desk and went for coffee. Chen looked at the folder for a long time. The old thought came: he could simply not mention the exam summary he'd found in the shared drive.

Instead he tore out the table page and wrote one line at the top of a fresh one: "Better than last month on thermodynamics."

When Oskar came back, Chen said, "The summary is in the blue tab. Use it." Oskar blinked. "Swap mock papers tonight?" They did, and later argued cheerfully about a question neither could solve.

qa.q: What did Chen keep in his notebook?
qa.a: A small table comparing Oskar's rank, offers and package with a column for himself.

qa.q: What was going on in Chen's mind as he looked at the folder?
qa.a: Rivalry and envy. The old thought came that he could simply not mention the exam summary he had found.

qa.q: What does Chen's new one-line note do for him?
qa.a: It shifts the comparison to his own progress since last month, a fairer measure than Oskar's ranks and packages.

qa.q: How might Oskar have felt when Chen shared the summary?
qa.a: Surprised and glad. Asking to swap mock papers treats Chen as a fellow traveller rather than a rival.

grounding: Chen measures himself against Oskar in ranks and packages, then compares with his own yesterday and shares instead of hiding notes.

subtopic: Friend succeeds when you are struggling
passage:
"Ira, did you finish the aptitude mock?" Ritu dropped onto the hostel bed. "I got 68."
Irawati glanced at her own screen. 71. Her chest loosened, then tightened again. "Seventy-one."
"Ugh, you're always three ahead." Ritu laughed. "Which book are you using for puzzles? Mine's useless."
For a second Irawati thought of naming the old, outdated one. Just to stay ahead. She heard how that sounded in her head and felt sick.
"The green one on my shelf. Take it tonight, I'm done with puzzles."
"Seriously? Thanks."
"Can I tell you something embarrassing? I check your score before I check mine. I've been treating you like a scoreboard."
Ritu was quiet. "I do that too, sometimes."
"What if we just compare with last week's us? I got 64 last Sunday. So 71's good."
"I got 60. So 68 is great."
"See? We're both winning."

qa.q: What did Ritu score on the aptitude mock?
What did Irawati feel when tempted to name the outdated book?
qa.a: A pull to stay ahead, followed by feeling sick and ashamed at how that sounded.

qa.q: What change did Irawati suggest, and why does it help?
qa.a: Comparing with last week's score instead of with each other; it makes the friend a fellow traveller rather than a scoreboard.

qa.q: How does Ritu respond to Irawati's confession?
qa.a: She goes quiet, then admits she does it too sometimes, relieved that it is said aloud.

grounding: Shows measuring oneself against a friend in scores, nearly giving a false tip, and choosing to compare with one's own past instead.

subtopic: Friend succeeds when you are struggling
passage:
In placement season last year, Payal and I became a two-person league table. She'd get a shortlist; I'd refresh the portal until I had one too. When she got a 9-lakh offer and I got 7, I said "congrats" with a straight face and then didn't sleep.
The worst thing I did was small. Before her second interview she asked for my system design notes. I said I'd lost them. They were in my bag.
She cleared the interview anyway. And I felt ridiculous, because what had I won? Nothing, except being the kind of person who hides notes from a friend.
Now I keep a different list. Where was I last month? Last year? I didn't know recursion two years ago. Now I teach it to juniors. That comparison actually helps.
Last week I gave Payal the notes for her cousin and told her the truth about them. She said, "I know. Your bag was open."
— Chaitanya

qa.q: What did Chaitanya say about the system design notes?
qa.a: That they were lost, though they were in Chaitanya's bag.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya feel after Payal cleared the interview anyway?
qa.a: Ridiculous and ashamed, seeing that nothing had been won by hiding the notes.

qa.q: What new comparison does Chaitanya use, and why is it better?
qa.a: Comparing with last month or last year; it shows real growth, from not knowing recursion to teaching it, instead of a race with a friend.

qa.q: How did Payal see the "lost" notes?
qa.a: She knew the truth all along ("Your bag was open") but let it go, showing hurt and also patience.

grounding: Illustrates measuring oneself against a friend in offers, the harm of hiding notes, and comparing instead with one's own yesterday.
